title: Real New Orleans jazz versus fast Dixieland; symphony benefit
summary: They distinguish fast Dixieland from New Orleans jazz, and Martin recalls a show where the other band's members kept time to his.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: That's what I was telling you one other time, Tink, you may remember, why I kind of differentiate between what some people think of as Dixieland today and what we think of New Orleans jazz, all this fast stuff that they call Dixieland today, that's what I say, that's the Ringling Brothers, Barnum and Bailey version of New Orleans jazz.

That's not the real New Orleans jazz. No, we played, what was that affair that we played when we got, when all the actors and that came out, was it a hard fun or whatever it was? When we played with the band?
Oh, Save Your Symphony. Huh? That was the drive to save the symphony.
Victor Borghi was the star of the show.
Now, now there's boys that's really knowing, they're popular and everything else, and they've got plenty of work and everything else. But that tempo is fast tempo.

How about the last cross? Now, let me show you. Now, they're all musicians. All right. We get there and we start to play. Naturally, they played one number and we play another number. Well, the boys in the band could see what they were doing. This is what they were doing on the other side of the stage.
Keeping the hardwood upper. That goes to show you we made even them feel it.
Oh, they've always been some of our greatest fans. The Lansdrasse have always been the fans.
